lead: Every receiver adds its own noise. A weak signal enters with a signal-to-noise ratio and leaves with a worse one. Noise figure says how much worse. The cascade formula shows that the first amplifier decides almost everything, so a receiver is built front to back around it. Sensitivity is the smallest input signal that still leaves the demodulator the signal-to-noise ratio it needs. Every handset, Wi-Fi router and satellite receiver is specified with these numbers, and they close the link budget from Unit 2.
prereq: You need: dB, dBm and the Friis link budget from Unit 2, plus the thermal noise power kTB; the loss of real passive parts is in 5.1.

sections.h3: Noise factor, noise figure and noise temperature

blocks.text: A resistor at temperature T delivers available noise power kTB over a bandwidth B. Here k = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant and T is in kelvin. At the standard reference temperature T₀ = 290 K the noise density kT₀ is 4.0×10⁻²¹ W/Hz, which is −174 dBm in 1 Hz.

A two-port block — amplifier, mixer or filter — receives a signal with some signal-to-noise ratio and delivers it with a lower one, because the block adds noise of its own. The noise factor compares the two ratios.

blocks.where: SNR<sub>in</sub> and SNR<sub>out</sub> are input and output signal-to-noise ratios as power ratios, measured in the same bandwidth with the source at T₀ = 290 K; F is the noise factor, a plain ratio, ≥ 1 for any real block.

blocks.text: Noise figure is the same quantity in decibels. A block with F = 2 has NF = 3.01 dB. Because F ≥ 1, NF is never negative for a block at room temperature.

blocks.where: NF is the noise figure in dB; F is the linear noise factor.

blocks.text: Noise temperature says the same thing in kelvin. An amplifier with F = 1.585 has Te = (1.585 − 1) × 290 = 170 K. Sky noise and antenna noise are usually quoted this way.

blocks.where: Te is the equivalent noise temperature in kelvin; T₀ = 290 K is the reference; F is the linear noise factor.

items: dB is 10 log₁₀ of a power ratio; for voltages across equal resistance, 20 log₁₀ gives the same dB.
dBm is power relative to 1 mW: P(dBm) = 10 log₁₀(P / 1 mW); 0 dBm = 1 mW and −174 dBm = 4×10⁻²¹ W.
Linear power gain from dB: G = 10^(G<sub>dB</sub>/10); a 15 dB amplifier has G = 31.62.

blocks.where: F is the total noise factor of the chain, linear; F₁, F₂, F₃ are the noise factors of the stages, linear; G₁ and G₂ are the available power gains of stages 1 and 2 as linear ratios, never in dB.

blocks.text: Read the formula as a noise budget referred to the input. Stage 1 contributes all of its own noise. Stage 2's noise is divided by G₁, because stage 1 amplifies signal and noise together. Stage 3 is divided by G₁G₂ and usually vanishes.

items: Convert every stage's noise figure to a linear factor: F = 10^(NF/10).
Convert every stage's gain to a linear power ratio: G = 10^(G<sub>dB</sub>/10).
Substitute the linear numbers into the Friis formula.
Convert the result back with NF = 10 log₁₀ F.

blocks.text: The consequence is a design rule. A first amplifier with 20 dB gain (G₁ = 100) makes every later stage 100 times less important, so the low noise amplifier goes first (see 5.6). A passive part has loss L at T₀, so F = L and G = 1/L: its noise figure equals its loss in dB.
For a lossy filter placed first, followed by an amplifier, the cascade reduces neatly to NF = (loss in dB) + NF of the amplifier. The same filter after 20 dB of gain barely changes the total.
Sensitivity is the weakest input the receiver can use. Start from the thermal noise in the channel, add the receiver's own noise, then the margin the demodulator needs.
P<sub>min</sub> = −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log₁₀ B + NF + SNR<sub>min</sub>
blocks.where: P<sub>min</sub> is the minimum usable input power in dBm; B is the channel bandwidth in Hz; NF is the receiver noise figure in dB; SNR<sub>min</sub> is the signal-to-noise ratio the demodulator requires, in dB.

items: −174 dBm is kT₀ in 1 Hz, the noise floor at 290 K.
Adding 10 log₁₀ B widens that floor to the channel.
Adding NF is the noise the receiver itself contributes.
Adding SNR<sub>min</sub> gives the input power that leaves enough margin at the detector.

blocks.text: Each factor of 10 in bandwidth costs 10 dB, so a 10 MHz channel sits 70 dB above a 1 Hz one. Halving the bandwidth buys 3 dB of sensitivity, which is why narrowband links reach further. Handset sensitivity is written into cellular standards, and GNSS signals arrive below −130 dBm.

items: Adjacent-channel rejection (ACR) is the attenuation in dB that the receiver gives to a signal in the next channel; the IF filter sets it.
Alternate-channel rejection (AACR) is the same figure for the channel two channels away, again a filter selectivity number.

figure.caption: The chain used in the worked example: LNA, mixer and IF amplifier with their gains and noise figures. Notice the LNA's 15 dB gain shrinking the mixer's 12 dB noise figure to a small share of the total.

spec.aria: A source drives an LNA, then a mixer, then an IF amplifier, with gain and noise figure values used in the cascade calculation.

examples.question: An LNA has G₁ = 15 dB and F₁ = 2 dB. A mixer has G₂ = 10 dB and F₂ = 12 dB. An IF amplifier has G₃ = 20 dB and F₃ = 10 dB. Find the cascaded noise figure of the chain, and its sensitivity for a channel bandwidth B = 10 MHz when the demodulator needs SNR = 10 dB.
steps: Linear gains: G₁ = 10^(15/10) = 31.62, G₂ = 10^(10/10) = 10; G₃ is not needed, it is the last stage.
Channel noise: 10 log₁₀(10 × 10⁶) = 70 dB, so N = −174 + 70 + 3.19 = −100.81 dBm.
Add the required SNR: P_min = −100.81 + 10 = −90.81 dBm, about 0.83 pW.
examples.answer: The cascaded noise figure is F = 2.083, that is NF = 3.19 dB, and the sensitivity is P_min = −90.81 dBm (about 0.83 pW).
examples.check:
import math
NF1, GdB1 = 2.0, 15.0
NF2, GdB2 = 12.0, 10.0
NF3, GdB3 = 10.0, 20.0
B = 10e6
SNRmin = 10.0
F1 = 10**(NF1/10); G1 = 10**(GdB1/10)
F2 = 10**(NF2/10); G2 = 10**(GdB2/10)
F3 = 10**(NF3/10)
F = F1 + (F2-1)/G1 + (F3-1)/(G1*G2)
NF = 10*math.log10(F)
noise = -174 + 10*math.log10(B) + NF
Pmin = noise + SNRmin
print(round(F, 3))
print(round(NF, 2))
print(round(Pmin, 2))

traps: Adding noise figures directly in dB. 2 dB followed by 12 dB is not 14 dB; convert to linear factors, use Friis, convert back.
Putting dB gains into the Friis denominator. That G₁ must be 31.62, not 15.
Confusing noise factor with noise figure. F = 2.083 is a ratio; NF = 3.19 dB is the same number in decibels.
Forgetting a lossy filter in front. A passive loss L has F = L and G = 1/L, so a 3 dB filter first adds 3 dB straight onto the system figure.
Using −174 dBm as the total noise power. It is per hertz, so 10 log₁₀ B must always be added.
Mixing sensitivity with dynamic range. Sensitivity is the weak end set by noise; the strong end is set by compression and intermodulation (see 5.3).

quiz.q: Define noise figure and give the relation between noise factor F and noise temperature Te.
quiz.a: Noise figure is NF = 10 log₁₀ F, where F = SNR_in/SNR_out for a block with its source at T₀ = 290 K. The relation is Te = (F − 1)T₀, or F = 1 + Te/T₀.

quiz.q: Why does the first stage of a receiver decide the cascaded noise figure?
quiz.a: Every later stage's noise is divided by the gain that precedes it before it is referred to the input. After a first stage gain G₁, the second stage contributes only (F₂ − 1)/G₁, and the third only (F₃ − 1)/(G₁G₂). Large front-end gain makes those terms small.

quiz.q: A 3 dB lossy filter sits in front of an amplifier with NF = 1.5 dB. Find the system noise figure.
quiz.a: Filter: F = 10^(3/10) = 2, G = 1/2 = 0.5. Amplifier: F = 10^(0.15) = 1.413. Friis: F = 2 + (1.413 − 1)/0.5 = 2 + 0.825 = 2.825. NF = 10 log₁₀(2.825) = 4.51 dB, which is the 3 dB loss plus the 1.5 dB amplifier figure.

quiz.q: A receiver has B = 200 kHz, NF = 6 dB and needs SNR_min = 9 dB. Find its sensitivity.
Two designs use the same three stages but swap the order of a 3 dB filter and a 15 dB LNA. Compare their noise figures.
quiz.a: Filter first: F = 2 + (1.585 − 1)/0.5 = 3.17, so NF = 10 log₁₀(3.17) = 5.01 dB. LNA first: F = 1.585 + (2 − 1)/31.62 + later terms divided by 31.62 × 0.5 = 1.585 + 0.032 = 1.617, so NF = 10 log₁₀(1.617) = 2.09 dB. The amplifier-first order wins by about 2.9 dB, close to 3 dB.

quiz.q: What do ACR and AACR measure, and what sets them?
quiz.a: ACR is the attenuation in dB given to a signal in the adjacent channel; AACR is the same for the alternate channel, two channels away. Both are filter selectivity figures, set mainly by the IF filter.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, noise figure is measured with a noise-figure analyser using the Y-factor method: a noise source switches between two known temperatures and the ratio of the two output powers gives F. When a block is not a clean 50 Ω two-port, designers use noise correlation matrices instead of a single F. Cascaded noise and sensitivity appear in cellular reference-sensitivity and blocking requirements, in GNSS receivers and in radio astronomy. Search next: Y-factor noise measurement, noise correlation matrix, minimum detectable signal.
